tier_reason: REPORT.md matches the claim exactly: median 9,023,597 vs 2,066,099 deliveries/s against nats-server v2.14.6, 4.37x, and 76.4% less server CPU. The harness is public (profiling/bench/run.py driving the Go client profiling/bench/main.go), and the CPU (Ryzen 7 9700X) and affinity are stated. The rustc version is never stated (no rust-toolchain file; the README only says 'a toolchain that supports the 2024 edition'), so by the rustc-version precedent this is first-party with partial methodology: C, not A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: cargo build --release --locked, using the default release profile (opt-level 3) with debug=true in Cargo.toml, no custom RUSTFLAGS and Rust 2024 edition; the rustc version is not stated anywhere
corrections.hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 9700X, single Linux host over loopback TCP; server pinned to CPUs 0-3,8-11 and the Go benchmark client to 4-7,12-15 (4 physical cores/8 logical each); fd limit 1,048,576
corrections.caveats: Very new, low-visibility repo (2 stars). It has no LICENSE file, so the code cannot legally be reused. The rustc version is not stated. The measurement is a single host over loopback with 3 runs per server, and the report says the host 'runs other services'. The runs are finite bursts, not steady state, and the author notes they do not establish performance on other hardware or over a real network. Wisp implements only part of NATS Core (no clustering, no JetStream), so the comparison covers only the core pub/sub fan-out path. The earlier 100-subscriber comparison in the same repo showed a smaller ~2.6x lead.

notes: Language mismatch: this came from a search filtered to C++, but Wisp is a Rust NATS-protocol server. It is judged on its merits. The claimed tier A is not supported with only 2 stars and an unpinned toolchain. The numbers are real and well documented (env hashes, alternating server order, warmups), so keep it at C, tagged reference-only (no license).

tier_reason: The blog states the Kafka ratios directly: Zenoh peer mode gets 65x Kafka's bitrate at 8B, 24x at the 8KB peak and 10x at 32KB (single machine). The Ryzen 7 5800X and the component versions are given, but no compiler or flags are stated in the blog or in the arXiv 2303.09419 v1 preprint. The linked benchmark code (github.com/ZettaScaleLabs/zenoh-perf/tree/master/comparison) now returns 404 on both the GitHub API and github.com. With no public code, no compiler, and a preprint that is not peer-reviewed (no journal-ref) published on the vendor's blog, this cannot be A or B, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Single-machine bitrate, Zenoh peer mode vs Kafka 3.2.1 (rdkafka 0.28.0 client): 65x at 8B payload, 24x at Zenoh's 8KB peak, 10x at 32KB (all stated on page). Multi-machine 100GbE: best ~50 Gbps (P2P) / ~34 Gbps (brokered) vs Kafka's best 5 Gbps, i.e. ~10x / ~6.8x (derived from page data)
corrections.caveats: Contributed by a National Taiwan University team but published on Zenoh's own blog, with a foreword by the Zenoh lead, so it is not arm's-length. The benchmark code repo cited by both the blog and the paper (ZettaScaleLabs/zenoh-perf, comparison/) is now 404, so the results cannot be reproduced from public code. No compiler versions or flags are stated. The arXiv 2303.09419 companion is a v1 preprint, not peer-reviewed. The headline ratios pit Zenoh peer-to-peer mode against brokered Kafka (Zenoh brokered mode also wins, by less). The tested Zenoh 0.7.0-rc dates from 2023. Kafka could not be measured above 512KB because the Rust Kafka binding failed on messages over 1MB.

notes: The original benchmark_url (zenoh-web blob/main/...) was 404 because the repo's default branch is master. I replaced it with the published zenoh.io page, which is identical to blob/master. The last commit on the default branch is 2026-09-15 (pushed_at 2026-09-25 is from another branch). License confirmed as EPL-2.0 OR Apache-2.0 (Cargo.toml SPDX and LICENSE).

tier_reason: docs/PERFORMANCE.md (results dated 2025-11-24) shows 476K avg and 554K peak msg/s vs Apache Kafka at 370K msg/s (+28.6% / +49.6%), and 0.002 vs 0.003 ms latency. A comparison harness exists (benchmark-suite/runners/run_comparison.sh, fluxmq-java-tests MultiThreadBenchmark), but no CPU, record size or partition count is given, and the Kafka version is not tied to the numbers. That is first-party with partial methodology, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: 476K msg/sec average (+28.6%) and 554K msg/sec peak (+49.6%) vs Apache Kafka at 370K msg/sec in the page's comparison table (results dated 2025-11-24); 0.002 ms vs 0.003 ms latency (-33.3%)
corrections.caveats: No CPU/hardware is stated for the cited numbers. The README is heavily marketing-styled. The repo's harness installs Kafka 3.9.0 (benchmark-suite/setup/install_kafka.sh), but the page never says which Kafka version, tuning or dataset produced the 370K figure, and no raw results are committed. The FluxMQ-tuned client config uses acks=0, lz4, 1MB batches and linger 15ms. The 0.002 ms 'latency' looks like amortized per-message time, not end-to-end latency. Treat as an unverified first-party claim.

notes: Language mismatch: this came from a search filtered to C++, but FluxMQ is a Rust Kafka-protocol broker. Metadata checks out (MIT, 8 stars, not a fork, last commit 2026-03-20, active). The win is small (+29%) and poorly documented but real as claimed, so C stands.
